In many programming languages (including C and C++), when we divide two integers the result is also an integer value with any remainder discarded or "truncated". This process of division where only the quotient is returned without considering the remainder is known as *integer division*. 
C/C++ provide us a variety of built-in data types to work with numbers, and one such type that we use for integers in C/C++ programming language is int. The size of an integer varies from machine to machine depending on the architecture but it must be at least capable of holding values between -32768 to 32767 (or within a similar range like signed short, long or any other integral type).

Here's an example code snippet that demonstrates how to use integers and their divison operation with c++ compiler. Note here, I have used int data type variables but you can replace this by any other integer datatype provided your system supports those datatypes as well (e.g., short, long etc.):

```cpp
      /* Perform integer division */

    return 0;                        }                             
```
In the example above I am first initializing x and y as integers having values `20`and `3`, respectively. Next, we perform division operation between these two variables 'x' and 'y'. Since both operands are integer types (int), result is also an integer value which discards or truncates any remainder that might be there in the actual mathematical quotient for those numbers. Finally I print this computed Integer divided with some format specifier '%f', it will convert int type to double before printing if needed and display output as decimal number 6.6667 (repeating).

This is because in computer programming languages by default everything behaves like integers only until you specify explicitly to treat something else.
To overcome this caveat (or limitation), we can cast one or both operands into double type before doing division operation so that the compiler treats them as real numbers not just whole integer values anymore allowing us get actual quotient including decimal part if needed too !  let's change our sample code slightly then:   ```cpp
